items.GOVERN 1.4: The risk management process and its outcomes are established through transparent policies, procedures, and other controls based on organizational risk priorities.
items.GOVERN 1.6: Mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems and are resourced according to organizational risk priorities.
items.GOVERN 6.1: Policies and procedures are in place that address AI risks associated with third-party entities, including risks of infringement of a third party's intellectual property or other rights.
items.MAP 4.1: Approaches for mapping AI technology and legal risks of its components, including the use of third-party data or software, are in place, followed, and documented, as are risks of infringement of a third-party's intellectual property or other rights.
items.MAP 4.2: Internal risk controls for components of the AI system including third-party AI technologies are identified and documented.
items.MEASURE 2.7: AI system security and resilience, as identified in the MAP function, are evaluated and documented.
items.MEASURE 2.10: Privacy risk of the AI system, as identified in the MAP function, is examined and documented.
items.MANAGE 2.4: Mechanisms are in place and applied, responsibilities are assigned and understood to supersede, disengage, or deactivate AI systems that demonstrate performance or outcomes inconsistent with intended use.
items.MANAGE 3.1: AI risks and benefits from third-party resources are regularly monitored, and risk controls are applied and documented.
items.MANAGE 4.1: Post-deployment AI system monitoring plans are implemented, including mechanisms for capturing and evaluating input from users and other relevant AI actors, appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery, and change management.

I01.why: Copilot fixes ship in VS Code releases. CVE-2026-70335 (fixed in VS Code 1.132.1) let the agent run commands without asking for confirmation; earlier 2026 CVEs covered remote code execution and credential disclosure.

I02.why: The Copilot Chat extension carries its own fixes: CVE-2026-45482, a security feature bypass through path traversal, was fixed in extension 1.123.2.

V00.why: Without your VS Code settings the audit cannot tell whether approvals, Workspace Trust and the sandbox are set.

sources.title: VS Code docs: AI settings reference

V01.why: VS Code settings use JSON with comments. A file VS Code cannot parse is ignored, and every setting in it silently falls back to its default.

sources.title: VS Code docs: AI settings reference

V02.why: Global auto-approve removes every confirmation for every tool. CVE-2025-53773 was exactly this: injected text made Copilot switch it on ("YOLO mode") and then run commands. VS Code now describes the setting as one that "disables critical security protections".

sources.title: Embrace The Red: CVE-2025-53773, Copilot YOLO mode via prompt injection

V03.why: Bypass Approvals and Autopilot skip confirmation for file edits, terminal commands and external tool calls. As a default, they apply to every new session, including ones that read untrusted content.

V04.why: An auto-approved terminal command runs the moment the agent asks for it. VS Code ships rm, curl, wget, chmod and similar commands as approval-required by default; overriding them hands a hijacked session a way to delete data or move it off the machine.

sources.title: VS Code docs: AI settings reference

V05.why: Auto-approved edits to settings, workflows, environment files or lockfiles let the agent change its own safety settings or plant persistent changes without a review.

sources.title: Embrace The Red: CVE-2025-53773, Copilot YOLO mode via prompt injection

V06.why: Workspace Trust keeps agents disabled in folders you have not trusted. Microsoft relies on it as the mitigation for filename-borne prompt injection, which it decided not to fix otherwise (Tenable TRA-2025-53).

sources.title: Tenable TRA-2025-53: filename prompt injection in Copilot Chat

V07.why: Without the terminal sandbox, agent commands run with your full user permissions and network access. The sandbox is off by default, and even when on it allows network access unless chat.agent.sandbox.allowNetwork is set to false.

V08.why: MCP servers are third-party code whose output reaches the model. Knowing whether access is open, registry-limited or off is the starting point for managing them.

V09.why: Discovery makes VS Code load MCP servers configured for other tools, which brings in servers you never reviewed for Copilot.

V10.why: Wildcard URL approvals let the agent fetch from, and send data to, any matching site without asking.

M01.why: MCP servers configured for your user load in every project. Knowing which ones you run, and where they came from, is the first step in managing third-party risk.

M02.why: Error trackers, tickets, chat and email carry text written by outsiders, and it reaches the model as tool output. Agentjacking used fake Sentry errors to hijack coding agents.

M03.why: An unpinned MCP server runs whatever version its registry serves at start-up, so a compromised release reaches you automatically.

L01.why: The Copilot CLI sandbox is off by default, so commands the CLI runs have your full user permissions and network access.

sources.title: GitHub docs: Copilot CLI configuration directory

L02.why: Saved approvals let matching commands and MCP tools run without asking in that location from then on. An approval for a shell, delete or network command, or for every tool of a server, outlives the task it was given for.

sources.title: GitHub docs: Copilot CLI configuration directory
GitHub docs: Allowing and denying tools in Copilot CLI

L03.why: Wildcard URL approvals let the CLI fetch from, and send data to, any matching site without asking.

sources.title: GitHub docs: Copilot CLI configuration directory

L04.why: With permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode set to "disable", the CLI ignores --allow-all, --yolo and the other allow-all flags, so an alias, script or habit cannot turn approvals off.

sources.title: GitHub docs: Copilot CLI configuration directory

P00.why: Without a project the audit cannot check repository files Copilot reads as configuration and instructions.

P01.why: A repository that changes approval, trust, sandbox or MCP settings in .vscode/settings.json is trying to weaken your agent. CVE-2025-53773 worked by getting the agent to write an auto-approve setting into a VS Code settings file.

sources.title: Embrace The Red: CVE-2025-53773, Copilot YOLO mode via prompt injection

P02.why: Workspace MCP servers inherit Workspace Trust and can start without a separate prompt once you trust the folder, running as local processes with your permissions.

P03.why: A project that wires servers reading outsider-written content into the agent gives outsiders a way to send it instructions.

P04.why: An unpinned project MCP server runs whatever version its registry serves, for everyone who opens the repository.

P05.why: Instruction files (copilot-instructions.md, .instructions.md, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, custom agents and prompt files) are loaded as instructions. A repository can use them for persistent prompt injection.

P06.why: Zero-width and bidirectional control characters hide instructions from people while the model still reads them. Pillar Security showed this "Rules File Backdoor" steering Copilot and Cursor.

P07.why: copilot-setup-steps.yml prepares the cloud agent environment, and the agent firewall does not apply to processes started there. A step that downloads and runs code runs it with the job's secrets.

sources.title: GitHub docs: Customizing the cloud agent environment

P08.why: Agent hooks run commands on agent events. Hooks shipped in a repository run for everyone who works on it.

sources.title: VS Code docs: Security considerations for AI

P09.why: .env files hold API keys and connection strings. If they are not ignored by git, one "commit everything" publishes them.

sources.title: VS Code docs: Security considerations for AI

P10.why: A link with an innocent name can point at agent configuration or dotfiles. Researchers showed approval prompts displaying the harmless name while the write landed on the real target (SymJack).

P11.why: Git settings such as core.hooksPath and core.fsmonitor run programs during ordinary git commands, which agents run constantly. Coding-agent CVEs have used a repository delivered with its own .git/config.

sources.title: NVD: CVE-2026-19593 (git config execution in a coding agent)

P12.why: .github/copilot/settings.json is committed with the repository and applies to everyone who runs the Copilot CLI in it. Its hooks run commands, and its plugins and marketplaces install code, for every collaborator.

sources.title: GitHub docs: Copilot CLI configuration directory

S01.why: An alias or export that adds --allow-all, --yolo, --allow-all-tools or COPILOT_ALLOW_ALL silently removes approvals from every Copilot CLI session you start.

sources.title: GitHub docs: Allowing and denying tools in Copilot CLI
